After looking over the smart contracts I've noticed a few vulnerabilities within the contract.

Centralized risk medium: The Kill Switch feature in SparkLend is designed to stop new borrowing but still lets users add more collateral, repay loans, or withdraw their funds. This can usually be done by setting the Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratio to zero, which means the collateral can't be used to get more loans, but there's an easier way to do it by just turning off borrowing for each asset. When LTV is set to zero, any new collateral can't be used to back loans. This means users can only add to their existing collateral, not use new collateral. On the other hand, just turning off borrowing still allows users to add new collateral.  Centralized risk high: The KillSwitchOracle is a tool that goes through all the markets to stop any new borrowing. But there's a potential problem. If the governance (the group or process that makes decisions) has scheduled a plan to add a new asset or change the loan rules for an existing asset, this plan might still go through even after the Kill Switch has been activated. This is because of a feature called DSPause.exec(), which can execute these plans without needing permission again. Bad contract: The README says all borrowable assets are frozen, but only borrow-only assets actually get frozen. Additionally, there's a function called reset() that has a misleading description saying it resets everything, but it only resets a part of the contract.

Centralized risk medium: There's a problem with the SparkLend system where the address of the pool (a central part of the system) might not match the address set in the configurator (the tool used to set it up). If these addresses are different, a part of the system called SparkLendFreezerMom might not work correctly. This mismatch can create issues because the system relies on the correct address being used to function properly, and if it doesn't, the system could behave unexpectedly or fail.

External dependencies: The CappedOracle function always returns a price with 8 decimal places, no matter what the actual source's decimal places are. This is a problem because if the source, like the Chainlink price oracle, has a different number of decimal places (like 18 for ETH pairs), it causes a mismatch.
